title: Choose a single reasoning path, sampled agreement, or explicit search according to task verifiability and inference cost rather than trust in a convincing trace

questions.prompt: Several sampled reasoning paths for a logic problem produce the same final answer and convincing explanations. Self-consistency selects that answer by majority vote. Why does this agreement still require an independent correctness check?
options: The samples may repeat the same misconception, so a wrong answer can win the vote.
The vote gives longer explanations more weight, so verbosity can outweigh a correct answer.
The vote groups intermediate steps, so different valid routes can split support for one answer.
The samples prune partial solutions, so an evaluator can discard the branch containing the correct answer.

rubric.point: Recognises that correlated errors can produce agreement on an incorrect answer.

questions.model: The samples may repeat the same misconception, so a wrong answer can win the vote.

questions.prompt: A scheduling puzzle requires assigning jobs to time slots under fixed constraints. Some early assignments lead to dead ends only after further jobs are assigned. A reliable checker can identify a dead end from a partial schedule. Explain what explicit search with branching and backtracking can do here that sampling complete solutions and voting on their final answers does not.

rubric.point: Explains that search can check partial schedules and stop expanding branches identified as dead ends.
Explains that search can return to an earlier partial schedule and try another assignment, whereas final-answer voting only aggregates completed paths.

questions.model: Search checks partial schedules and stops expanding dead ends. It can then return to an earlier schedule and try another assignment; final-answer voting only compares completed paths.
